I never intended to tell this story to anyone, but if that bastard is going to get me I won’t go down in silence.

It’s been a long time since I believed in ghosts, goblins, ghouls, demons, devils, or gods. That wasn’t always the case though; once upon a time I was sure I’d grow up to devote my life in service to God’s work. The man who inspired that dream also stole my childhood and betrayed a sacred trust. Pastor Matthews ripped my faith from me.

He paid for it. There was a trial; it made national news, and there were rumors of more than a dozen kids abused by this so-called holy man. Only four of us actually testified against him when the time came, but it was more than enough to put the bastard away. Names were kept out of the papers, of course, to allow us to lead normal lives. He got 25-to-life and I got a lifetime of psychiatrist bills.

That was nine years ago, and I’ve tried to put it behind me. I’m the first to admit I haven’t done a very good job. When I heard six weeks ago that my abuser had been found stabbed in his cell, I felt like I had won the lottery. I’m not proud of that fact, but I was overjoyed. I called in sick to work just to attend his funeral. I guess I wanted to face him one last time before they put him in the ground for good. I wasn’t alone. When I arrived I saw half a dozen kids from my old church, now grown into young adults themselves, including two others who had testified against Pastor Matthews. We didn’t look each other in the eye, but I could tell I wasn’t the only one hiding a smile.

The viewing was hard, much more so than I would have expected. His body was laid out and dressed in a suit as fine as any he had worn during a Sunday sermon. The funeral home had done a great job, and he looked at peace. It was irrational, but I couldn’t help feeling like he looked like he had won. I wanted to grab him by his well-pressed lapels and scream at him. It might have happened too, if not for the young woman sobbing behind me. I knew it was his daughter, and I knew during the trial she had testified he never laid a finger on her. Shaking with anger, I turned away from my one-time mentor.

Only to see him staring at me through the large bay window at the far end of the funeral home’s viewing room. I swear it was him. Bald head, tailored suit, genial smile. I turned back to look at the corpse in the coffin. It was, of course, still right where it should be. When I turned back to the window, he was gone. I couldn’t wipe the image of that smile, the same smile he’d always given me when I came to him for advice, staring at me.

Shock had doused the fire of my anger, and I nearly jumped out of my skin when a voice spoke up behind me.

“You saw him?” A familiar voice spoke behind me. I couldn’t place it, not in my panicked state.

“Him who?” I didn’t take my eyes off the window to see who had asked, and the strain had pushed my voice up an octave.

When I didn’t get an answer, I turned around. No one was there. I was starting to think it was all some kind of joke. A sick little game perpetrated by someone who had always believed we made the whole thing up. There were more than a few people who still insisted the pastor would never have done what we said he did. I went home, showered, and went to bed early. Going to the funeral was a mistake, but it was over and life could go on. That was what I believed, until the next morning when I saw the news.

Henry. It was his voice at the funeral asking me what I had seen. We had talked about entering seminary together when we were kids. Before the trial, and the horrible things that lead up to it, we had made plans. His family moved away the first chance they got though, and we had lost touch. I never knew he’d moved back to town.

Now he was dead.

They were calling it a homicide. I hopped online to try and find out more information, but all the police would say was that it was an ongoing investigation. I thought about calling the tip line and telling them about what I had seen at the funeral, but what could I say? “Hello officer, I think I saw him being followed by a dead man yesterday.”

I shook it off and went into work. The day was normal enough though twice I looked out the window and thought I saw Pastor Matthews across the street.

That night I saw him again. He was standing across the street from my apartment. I live on the third floor, but I could see him and he was looking straight at me. For the first time in almost a decade, I whispered a prayer and hoped somebody was listening. I did call the police then, I told them there was a suspicious man hanging around my complex. A patrol car came by a bit later and two cops got out with their flashlights. They passed by Pastor Matthews twice without saying a word. When they couldn’t find anything, they left.

I watched it all from my window, and he watched me watching. That friendly smile never left his face.

I see him everywhere now. There have been two more murders in town. I didn’t know the names, but I recognized the faces. They were the other kids who testified. I’m the last one.

Today I started seeing him in my mirror. I took a hammer to it and shattered it into a million pieces, but I could see his face reflected in every broken shard. His smile seems less friendly now; there are too many teeth. I don’t remember him having so many teeth.

I’m not looking for pity or help. It’s too late for me, and I think he’ll be finished when I’m gone. There’s no one else to take his revenge on. I’ve made my peace with God. In a funny way, he’s given me back the most precious thing he took from me, my faith. I just want the world to know what he did. I want everyone to know that he’s still a sick sadistic son of a bitch. Death didn’t do anything to change that.
